steps.action:
# The Last Light

Every evening at dusk, Margaret climbed the spiral stairs.

She had counted them once, back in 1987, during a storm so violent she needed something to occupy her hands between the thunderclaps. Two hundred and twelve steps. She had never counted them again. Some numbers, once learned, become part of your breathing.

The lighthouse stood on a finger of rock that pointed accusingly into the North Atlantic, as though blaming the ocean for something old and unforgivable. Margaret had come here after her husband died, taking the posting because no one else wanted it, and because she needed a place where the wind was louder than her thoughts.

That first winter nearly broke her. The isolation was a physical weight, something she wore on her shoulders like a wet coat. Supply boats came once a month. She talked to the radio. She talked to the gulls. Eventually, she just talked to herself and stopped being embarrassed about it.

But somewhere in that second year, something shifted.

She began to understand that the light wasn't for her. That was the secret of the work — its beautiful selflessness. Every night she maintained the lamp, checked the lens, logged the weather, and sent that steady pulse out into the blackness for *other people*. Fishermen she'd never meet. Sailors navigating by instruments who would never know her name.

She kept them safe without ever knowing she had.

On her last night before retirement, a young man from the coastal authority came to observe the transition. He watched her move through her routine with quiet efficiency — unhurried, deliberate, absolutely certain.

"Weren't you ever lonely out here?" he asked.

Margaret looked out at the beam sweeping across the dark water.

"Every single day," she said. "But loneliness and purpose can live in the same house. You just have to give them separate rooms."

She handed him the logbook. It was heavier than he expected.
